summary: Inspected Sage workspace markup and CSS and researched authoritative landmark, keyboard, responsive grid, dialog, and overflow guidance for a study workspace with plan/quiz, chat, and artifact rails.

findings.topic: Current workspace DOM and semantic structure
findings.conclusion: static/sage-workspace.html has one static h1 in the header, a div.layout containing an unlabeled aside.sidebar, a main.main containing the chat and an aside.diagram-panel. The plan is currently the third sidebar section after Sessions and Files. The quiz is generated as an article inside the artifact rail, while the composer has a Quiz button. The artifact aside explicitly sets role=complementary even though aside already has the implicit complementary role.
findings.source: Local inspection: static/sage-workspace.html lines 203-280 and dynamic artifact construction around lines 580-680

findings.conclusion: The workspace currently uses nested flex containers: .app and .layout are fixed to the viewport with overflow hidden; .sidebar has overflow-y:auto; .chat has overflow:hidden and .chat__messages has overflow-y:auto; .diagram-panel has overflow:hidden and .diagram-panel__body has overflow:auto. At max-width:1023px, the sidebar is absolutely positioned as an overlay and the diagram panel becomes an absolutely positioned panel up to 60vh. This works as a desktop split/overlay model but creates multiple independent scroll containers and makes mobile rail focus/visibility state dependent on custom class toggles.

The workspace has a single structural breakpoint at max-width:1023px and a reduced mobile padding breakpoint at max-width:767px. Therefore 640 and 768 both receive the overlay behavior, 1024 is the first desktop split width, and 1280 receives the full three-part layout only if the artifact rail is open. The existing 1023 threshold is not inherently wrong, but it should be paired with explicit 640/768/1024/1280 acceptance checks rather than treating 1024 as mobile by accident.
findings.source: Local inspection: static/sage-workspace.html lines 199-200; static/style.css lines 803-817

findings.conclusion: CSS Grid is the better primitive for the top-level desktop workspace because it expresses a two-dimensional rail/chat/rail relationship with explicit tracks and named areas; Flexbox remains appropriate inside each rail, the chat column, and the composer because those are one-dimensional flows. Use minmax(0, 1fr) for the chat track and min-width:0 on the grid/flex children so message content cannot force horizontal overflow. Keep DOM/source order aligned with the intended reading and focus order; do not use order or grid placement to create a logical order that differs from source order.

Use progressive track changes instead of absolute-positioned desktop rails: at wide desktop, grid-template-columns can be a fixed plan rail, minmax(0,1fr), and a bounded support rail; at medium width, keep the plan rail and hide or make the support rail a triggerable sheet; at narrow widths, collapse to one column with the central chat as the only in-flow primary surface and expose plan/support as dialogs or bottom sheets. The exact pixel tracks should be chosen from content minima, not from a fixed three-column assumption.

Use one top-level main landmark for chat. A plan rail is a complementary landmark only when it remains meaningful alongside main; label it uniquely (for example, Study plan). A support/artifact rail is a second complementary landmark only when exposed as an independent persistent region; label it uniquely (for example, Artifacts and support). Avoid adding named region landmarks to every subsection: WAI-ARIA guidance says landmark value diminishes as their number grows and recommends meaningful labels for repeated landmark roles. A sidebar containing navigation links could instead be a nav landmark, but the study plan itself is better treated as complementary unless it is the application's primary navigation.

Keep exactly one page-level h1 for the session/workspace title in the header or main introduction. Generated message headings must not create competing page-level h1 elements; map assistant content to h2/h3 or render it inside a scoped article with an appropriate heading level. The main element itself should remain unique; a skip link can target it.

findings.topic: Keyboard focus order and source order
findings.conclusion: Place the DOM in the same task order users should tab through: header controls, plan rail, main chat/messages, composer, then support/artifacts, or use an intentional skip link to main and clearly documented rail controls. Do not rely on CSS order/grid placement to change logical order. Every rail toggle must be a native button with an accessible name, aria-expanded, and aria-controls. When a rail is hidden, remove it from the accessibility tree and tab sequence using hidden or inert rather than only opacity, visibility, pointer-events, or a zero width.

The existing Plan, Sessions, and Files section headers already approximate the disclosure pattern. Preserve native button controls, synchronize aria-expanded with visibility, and add aria-controls pointing at each controlled list. Enter and Space should operate without custom key handling. Keep the plan expanded by default or provide a clearly discoverable toggle because plan context is central to the study workflow.

Prefer one primary vertical scroll owner for the application surface: the message/content region. Keep the composer in a non-scrolling flex/grid row. Rails should normally fit and scroll only when their own content exceeds the viewport; their scroll containers need a visible accessible name and tabindex=0 if keyboard users must scroll them directly. Avoid making ancestors overflow:hidden solely to suppress scrollbars because hidden overflow can still create scroll containers and can obscure focus behavior; do not use overflow:clip around interactive content.

Do not allow body/app, layout, chat, messages, rail, panel body, and source previews all to compete as scroll owners. Recommended minimum is: document/app shell clips only the fixed chrome; main chat content owns vertical scrolling; each persistent rail owns a single internal vertical scroller only if needed; diagram/source code gets horizontal overflow locally. Add overscroll-behavior:contain only to intentional rail/panel scrollers to prevent scroll chaining, not as a substitute for clear ownership. Ensure focused controls scroll into view.

At 640 and 768, treat Plan and Artifacts/support as one-at-a-time bottom sheets over the chat, not simultaneous absolute sidebars. Use a native modal dialog for a blocking sheet (or a non-modal disclosure/popover only when the user must continue interacting with chat). A modal sheet needs a visible close button, Escape support, focus moved inside on open, focus returned to the invoking button on close, and inert background content. If the product wants to keep chat interactive behind the sheet, use a non-modal sheet and do not claim aria-modal=true. Sheet content should have one internal scroll owner and account for safe-area insets.
